account: Educational Initiatives ran three after-school Mindspark centers in Delhi. Sessions combined 45 minutes of adaptive exercises with 45 minutes of instruction in small groups. The software used teaching rules that specialists had written. A lottery offered 314 of 619 students a voucher that waived the fee. The authors of the final study report that voucher recipients gained 0.37 standard deviations in math and 0.23 in Hindi between September 2015 and February 2016. Average attendance was 58%, and 539 students completed endline tests. The estimate concerns the combined program. All three centers closed in March 2016 after enrollment remained below the threshold for continued subsidy. The authors argue that the gains most likely came from the software, because a contemporaneous after-school group tutoring trial in Delhi found no effect. In a working paper of 7 October 2025, Karthik Muralidharan and Abhijeet Singh report that an in-school version tested in Rajasthan public schools from late 2017 raised scores by 0.22 standard deviations in math and 0.20 in Hindi after 18 months. They report that this version has informed scale-ups that reach over 250,000 students in over 2,000 public schools.

ai_role.statement: Mindspark selected exercises using rules that education specialists wrote, and the trial evaluated it together with small-group instruction. The authors argue that the gains most likely came from the computer-aided part, because a contemporaneous trial of after-school group tutoring for middle-school students in Delhi, with longer sessions, found no effect on test scores. The trial did not measure the two parts separately.
